title: Top-Down vs Bottom-Up Sizing
description: Master the two core approaches to market sizing and learn when to apply each method.

interactions.prompt: A startup wants to estimate the U.S. dog food market. Which approach starts from the total population?

options.text: Top-down: start with total dog owners, narrow down
Bottom-up: start with one store, scale up
Competitive analysis: sum competitor revenues
Survey method: ask dog owners directly

interactions.teachingPreamble: Top-down sizing starts with a large known number (like total population) and narrows it using filters and percentages. For example, Chewy might size the U.S. pet food market by starting with 130M households, filtering to 65M dog-owning households, then multiplying by average annual spend.

interactions.prompt: A consultant estimates the U.S. yoga mat market two ways. Top-down (from fitness population): $1.8B. Bottom-up (from studio counts × purchases): $600M. What's the most important takeaway?

options.text: The top-down number is always more accurate
The 3x gap signals the top-down estimate likely overstates addressable demand
Average the two numbers to get the real answer
Bottom-up missed online sales, so ignore it

interactions.prompt: A food truck founder counts 3 office buildings nearby with 2,000 workers each. She estimates 10% buy lunch from trucks at $12 average. What is she doing?

options.text: Top-down sizing from national food truck revenue data
Bottom-up sizing from observable, ground-level unit economics
Calculating her TAM for the entire city
Conducting a break-even analysis

interactions.teachingPreamble: Bottom-up sizing builds from small, observable units - like individual customers, stores, or transactions - and scales up. It's grounded in real-world data you can verify. Sweetgreen used bottom-up logic early on: counting office workers near target locations and estimating capture rates to size each store's revenue potential.

interactions.prompt: Top-down sizing risks ____ the market because it starts broad and may use overly optimistic filter rates.

options.text: Underestimating
Overestimating
Segmenting
Ignoring

interactions.prompt: You're pitching investors for a new B2B SaaS tool targeting U.S. dental offices. You have time to prepare only one market sizing approach. Which do you choose?

options.text: Top-down from U.S. healthcare IT spending reports
Bottom-up from number of dental offices × likely spend per office
Competitor revenue analysis from public filings only
Survey 50 dentists and extrapolate nationally

interactions.prompt: When is top-down sizing most appropriate compared to bottom-up?

options.text: When you need a quick directional estimate of total market potential
When building a detailed financial model for year-one revenue
When pitching seed investors who want unit economics
When you have granular customer transaction data available

interactions.teachingPreamble: In practice, strong analysts use both approaches as a cross-check. Top-down is fastest for ballpark TAM estimates and works well when industry reports exist - like McKinsey sizing the global EV market at $460B. Bottom-up shines when you need credible, defensible numbers tied to specific customers and pricing.

interactions.prompt: Rank these steps for a solid bottom-up market size of a new premium coffee brand in Chicago, from first to last.

options.text: Multiply by average cups per customer per week
Identify total number of target neighborhoods
Apply your realistic capture rate percentage
Estimate premium coffee drinkers per neighborhood

interactions.prompt: Your competitor just raised $50M and is expanding into your target neighborhoods with aggressive discounts. How does this change your bottom-up market sizing?

options.text: No change - TAM stays the same regardless of competition
Your SAM/SOM estimates need lower capture rates to reflect competition
Switch entirely to top-down since bottom-up is now unreliable
Double your price to compensate for lost volume

interactions.priorContext: You previously sized the Chicago premium coffee market bottom-up using neighborhood counts, customer density, purchase frequency, and a capture rate. Now a well-funded competitor is entering the same neighborhoods.
